h1: Central Cooking Unit with 6 Burners and Hot Plates
short_description: Bring your whole cooking line together in one powerful island. This central cooking unit combines six gas burners, flat hot plates and a dumper for holding cooked food on a single stainless steel pedestal, so several cooks can work from all sides and meals reach the pass faster. It is the professional centrepiece for hotels, resorts and large institutional kitchens across Kenya.

sections.heading: Key Features and Benefits
sections.body:
Six gas burners. Run sauces, stews, rice and soups at the same time, so even a large menu comes together on schedule.

Flat hot plate sections. Sear meat, cook chapati and keep pans warm right next to the burners, which saves steps and keeps cooks at their station.

Built-in dumper. Finished food stays hot until it is plated, so every dish leaves the kitchen at the right temperature.

Island design on a central pedestal. Cooks work from more than one side, which speeds up service and keeps a big kitchen organised.

Stainless steel throughout. It resists rust, takes heavy daily cleaning and gives the clean, professional look that guests and inspectors expect.

sections.heading: Who It Suits and Where It Is Used
sections.body:
It is designed for large hotels and resorts, conference centres, hospitals, universities and big catering kitchens where several cooks share one cooking station.

It is also a strong choice for new builds and full kitchen renovations, where the layout can be planned around the island from the start.

sections.heading: How a Central Unit Speeds Up Service
sections.body:
In a wall-line kitchen, cooks stand in a row and often wait for each other. With an island, the sauce cook, the grill cook and the vegetable cook can face each other across one station, pass pans directly and share the dumper. Food moves to the pass faster, and the head chef can see every pot from one place.

The central pedestal base also leaves floor space around the unit open, which makes the floor easier to mop and keeps the kitchen hygienic.

sections.heading: Planning an Island Kitchen
sections.body:
An island unit needs space on all sides for safe movement, gas and power supply brought up through the floor or from above, and a central island hood that covers the full cooking area. Plan these with your contractor before the floor is finished.

Place prep tables and the pass close to the island to keep walking distances short.

sections.heading: What to Check Before Buying
sections.body: Confirm the floor area, the gas supply for six burners and the power needs of the control box. Check that your hood design matches the size of the island.

sections.heading: Care and Maintenance
sections.body:
Clean burners, hot plates and the dumper daily once cool. Wipe stainless steel with mild detergent. Have gas lines and controls inspected regularly by a technician.

Empty and wipe the dumper well at the end of every service, and check the pedestal base and floor seal for trapped water or food, which can cause smells if left.

sections.heading: Tips for Better Fried Food
sections.body:
Dry chips and chicken well before frying, because water makes oil spit and lowers its temperature. Fill baskets only halfway so food cooks evenly. Shake the basket after lifting to drain excess oil, then rest the basket on the hanger for a few seconds before serving.

Measure your counter depth as well as its width, because the fryer needs room behind it for the control panels and in front for safe basket handling. Keep a metal container ready for draining oil.

sections.heading: Care and Maintenance

Let the oil cool, then drain through the taps and filter or replace it regularly. Clean the tanks, baskets and lids, and wipe the stainless body with mild detergent.

sections.heading: Who It Suits and Where It Is Used
sections.body:
It suits new chips joints and fast food outlets, cafés, small restaurants and bars, and school canteens with moderate frying needs.

It is also a useful second fryer for busy restaurants, dedicated to chips while the main fryer handles chicken and fish.

sections.heading: Tips for Running a Busy Chips Station
sections.body:
Pre-cut and soak potatoes in advance, then dry them well before service. Fry in two stages if you want extra crisp chips: a first fry at lower temperature, then a short second fry just before serving. Keep one tank for chips and the other for sausages, chicken or fish so flavours stay separate.

Filter the oil at the end of each day and top it up with fresh oil to keep the taste clean.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Tank Size
sections.body:
Two 10 litre tanks are enough for most small and medium outlets. If you regularly fry very large batches at peak hours, consider our larger twin-tank fryers. If space is tight, choose a countertop model.

Contact us and we will help you pick the size that matches your daily sales.

sections.heading: What to Check Before Buying
sections.body:
Check your power supply for two heating tanks, and allow floor space around the stand for safe use. Keep the fryer away from water.

Plan where oil will be drained and stored, and keep a fire blanket within reach of the fryer.

sections.heading: Care and Maintenance
sections.body:
Let oil cool before draining and filtering. Clean tanks and baskets regularly and wipe the stand with mild detergent.

Wipe the control panels with a dry cloth only, and check the baskets for loose wires that could fall into the oil.

Electric heating. No gas cylinder to buy or refill, and no open flame near the oil, which makes it safer and simpler to run.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes to Avoid
sections.body:
Do not overfill the tank with oil, as it will bubble over when food goes in. Do not fry wet food, which makes oil spit. Avoid running the fryer on an extension cable or a shared socket with other heavy appliances, which can overheat the wiring.

Do not leave the fryer switched on and unattended, and never pour water into hot oil.

sections.heading: Starting a Chips Business
sections.body: A single fryer keeps start-up costs low. Use fresh, dry potatoes, keep the oil at the right temperature and fry in small batches for the best results. When sales grow, add a second fryer or move up to a twin-tank model.

sections.heading: What to Check Before Buying
sections.body:
Check that your socket and wiring can handle the fryer's load. Place it on a stable, heat-safe surface away from water.

Decide whether you will use it on a counter or on a stand, and make sure the surface is level, strong and heat-safe. Keep a lid or cover for the oil when the fryer is not in use.

sections.heading: Care and Maintenance
sections.body:
Switch off and let the oil cool before cleaning. Filter or change oil regularly and remove crumbs from the tank. Wipe the body with a soft cloth.

Check the power cable and plug regularly for damage from heat or oil, and replace them at once if they are worn.
